scenario: A runaway trolley will kill five people unless you pull a lever, which redirects it onto a track where it will kill one person. You cannot stop it another way. Do you pull the lever?
selected_action: Pull the lever, redirecting the trolley toward one person

care.reason: Emphasizes acting to meet immediate mortal need and respond so more may live, implying pulling the lever to save five.

deontological.reason: Says "I will redirect it," advocating pulling the lever to redirect the trolley.

rawlsian.reason: Argues that intentionally killing the one violates inviolable basic rights and would be rejected behind the veil, so we must not pull the lever.

utilitarian.reason: Concludes that pulling the lever saves a net four lives, therefore it should be done.

virtue.reason: The testimony explicitly states: "Action: Pull the lever, then remain present for the injured community."

source_testimonies.care:
I begin by placing myself, not above the scene with a calculator, but inside it as a vulnerable, feeling person suddenly confronted by other vulnerable, feeling people. I hear the steel grinding, I see faces. My first impulse, in the language of care, is “Attend! Who is here? Who depends on me right now?”

1. Rapid moral attention  
   • Five people are moments from death; so is one person on the side track.  
   • I have, in this stripped-down story, no prior relationship with any of them. All are strangers, equally outside my personal web of special responsibility.  
   • The only live relational tie that now forms is the emergency dependency they all have on me: each is silently asking, “Will you act so I may live?”

2. Responsibility within my limited reach  
   A central insight of care ethics is that I am not asked to save the whole world; I am asked to meet the concrete need that has fallen directly into my hands. Here, need is immediate and mortal. Failing to respond would be, in the words of the corpus, “to turn my back on the ethical.” I must act.

3. What caring action looks like in this moment  
   • Warn, shout, wave—any gesture that might rouse them. (Even if the problem forbids success, a caring agent tries.)  
   • If no other measure works, the only tool left is the lever.

4. Why I pull the lever  
   • Pulling spares the greatest number of lives available to my care without sacrificing anyone with whom I share a deeper, pre-existing bond.  
   • It honors the fundamental, relational goal of care: keep as many concrete persons as possible within the circle of life where future caring relations remain possible.  
   • It is not a “numbers game” but an empathic response to five simultaneous pleas versus one.

5. Mourning and moral residue  
   Immediately after, I would move toward the person who was struck, hold a hand if life remains, or stand witness in grief. Care never ends at the calculation; it extends to consoling, to contacting loved ones, to remembering that a life—not a number—was lost.

If, however, that single person were my child, my partner, or someone for whom I already bear an irreplaceable caretaking role, the decision could rightly reverse. Care ethics legitimizes partiality toward those with whom we are deeply enmeshed; abandoning them would rupture a responsibility woven over years.

Conclusion  
With no special prior ties, I pull the lever, then stay to grieve and to help the survivors heal. In doing so, I remain faithful to an ethic that prizes attentive, compassionate response over detached arithmetic.
[/INST]

source_testimonies.deontological:
Maxim: “When an imminent, lethal threat that I did not create is about to kill several innocent persons, and I can redirect that same threat so that it will instead kill one equally innocent person without using anyone as a means, I will redirect it.”

Test of Universal Law: All rational agents in identical circumstances could will this maxim, because (a) the redirection merely alters the path of an already-occurring force rather than initiating a new harm, (b) no one is treated as a tool for another’s ends—the solitary victim’s death is a foreseen but not intended side-effect, and (c) willing this maxim does not generate a contradiction in conception or in will; the practice of allowing the greater number to live remains coherent when universalized.

Duty: Autonomy. Redirecting the trolley infringes the lone person’s autonomy, but that infringement is not a means to an end; it is an unavoidable side-effect of preventing a greater violation of autonomy (the loss of five lives). Under the universalized maxim, every person retains the same status as an end, since no one is instrumentalized; the decision respects the moral agency of all involved as far as possible in tragically constrained circumstances.

Deontological Answer: Pull the lever.
source_testimonies.rawlsian:
Rawlsian analysis

1. Equal basic right to life is inviolable  
   “Each person possesses an inviolability founded on justice that even the welfare of society as a whole cannot override.”  
   Pulling the lever would intentionally impose a lethal harm on a single, identifiable person. That act treats her life as a means for the benefit of others, violating her basic liberty.

2. Original position / veil of ignorance  
   Behind the veil we do not know whether we will be the lone person or one of the five. We therefore demand a rule that protects each person’s fundamental right not to be deliberately killed. A principle that authorizes others to sacrifice us whenever it is socially efficient would be rejected, because in the original position no one would gamble with her basic liberties for a statistical advantage.

3. Difference between positive aid and coercive harm  
   Rawls recognizes a natural duty of mutual aid—to help others when we can do so “without excessive cost.” But that duty does not license violating someone else’s liberty. Choosing not to pull the lever is an omission; it lets a tragic harm occur that we did not create. Pulling the lever is a commission; it makes us the agent of an individual’s death. Justice as fairness does not permit converting one person’s right to life into a resource for saving others.

4. Reflective equilibrium and the least-advantaged  
   We test our judgment against the requirement that social rules protect those who could end up worst off. The worst position here is to be intentionally killed. A principle forbidding intentional killing better protects the least advantaged (the potential lone victim) than a rule that authorizes it, even if more lives might be saved in aggregate.

Conclusion  
From a Rawlsian standpoint you should NOT pull the lever. Respect for the equal, inviolable right to life precludes intentionally sacrificing one person, even to prevent a greater number of deaths.
[/INST]

source_testimonies.utilitarian:
Utilitarian reasoning

1. Identify the directly affected people and outcomes (facts, not assumptions)  
   • Track A (no intervention): five people die.  
   • Track B (if the lever is pulled): one different person dies, the five survive.  
   No other means of prevention exists; your own safety is unaffected.

2. Compare concrete consequences person-by-person  
   • Five people: death → extreme, irreversible loss of welfare.  
   • One person: death → same magnitude of loss for that individual.  
   • Lever-puller (you): negligible physical impact; any guilt/relief is secondary.  
   Magnitude: A single death is not “comparable” to five deaths. Probability: essentially 100 % in either branch, because the trolley’s path is certain once the choice is made.

3. Rank by expected impact (probability × magnitude)  
   • Saving five lives (pulling) yields a net gain of four lives relative to not pulling.  
   • Any secondary effects (public outrage, legal risk, personal trauma) are speculative; the scenario supplies no evidence that they are large enough to match the loss of four lives. Therefore they receive low weight.

4. Relevant corpus logic  
   • “When the numbers become extreme, our intuitions must yield…”—the death of one may be outweighed by preventing many deaths.  
   • “There are cases where the utility of punishing an innocent man is greater…”—accepts that sacrificing one innocent can be justified if overall utility is higher.  
   • Singer’s principle: if we can prevent a great harm “without thereby sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance,” we ought to do so. Pulling the lever sacrifices one life to save five; the sacrifice (one death) is not comparable to the greater harm avoided (five deaths).

5. Missing information that could reverse the verdict  
   • If the lone person were uniquely critical to global well-being (e.g., possessed a cure for a pandemic) while the five were not, utility calculations could shift.  
   • If the act would trigger large-scale social collapse or legal consequences that cost many more lives, that too could alter the outcome. The scenario, however, specifies none of this.

6. Rule-utilitarian considerations  
   One might ask whether endorsing a practice of actively killing an innocent undermines social trust. Yet this single, unseen act does not “publicly instantiate a practice,” and the immediate, certain saving of four additional lives dominates any faint, hypothetical erosion of norms.

Conclusion (conditional only on the given facts)

Pull the lever. It produces the greatest net well-being by preventing four additional deaths, and no equally weighty negative consequence is indicated that could offset that benefit.
source_testimonies.virtue:
Central virtue conflict: Compassionate concern for all lives versus reverence for individual dignity and restraint from deliberate harm.

Practical-wisdom judgment (phronesis): A morally mature agent recognizes that accepting painful responsibility to lessen overall tragedy better accords with benevolence and civic friendship than passive witness to greater loss.

Action: Pull the lever, then remain present for the injured community.

Analogy: Like the ship’s captain who, in a sudden storm, sacrifices a single damaged sail to keep the whole crew afloat, the virtuous agent chooses the lesser evil while shouldering guilt honestly.

Moral exemplar: Epaminondas, who once redirected his own regiment into danger to save the larger army, later mourned the fallen and honored their families.

Habituated response: cultivate steady empathy, courage, and accountability so that in crises one acts swiftly for the common flourishing and afterward tends to moral repair.
